subject: sr-english
title: If
author: Rudyard Kipling
instructions: Practice for this lesson in the question types of the April 2026 paper (new syllabus).
Where a question has OR, answer either one.
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.q: Why does Kipling describe 'Triumph' and 'Disaster' as 'impostors'?
options: They are permanent states of life
They deceive us into losing perspective
questions.answer: B

questions.q: 'Keep your head when all about you are losing theirs' means —
questions.answer: A

questions.q: How does the poem advise handling waiting, lies and hatred?
options: Wait impatiently and respond with lies
Be patient but repay hatred with hatred
Wait patiently, avoid lying and don't give in to hatred
questions.answer: D

questions.q: 'Build 'em up with worn-out tools' suggests —
options: starting again with whatever strength is left after a failure
finding a middle way in a conflict
questions.answer: B

questions.q: The repetition of 'If you can' at the beginning of lines is an example of —
questions.answer: A

questions.q: What best describes 'the Will' in the poem?
options: The spirit of never giving up against odds
questions.answer: A

questions.q: 'If—' is best described as a —
questions.answer: B

sections.title: Identify the following sentences as True or False.

questions.q: The speaker of the poem is a father advising his son.
questions.answer: A

questions.q: Kipling advises us to make dreams our master.
questions.answer: B
questions.note: 'If you can dream—and not make dreams your master.'

questions.q: The poet advises us to complain about our losses so others can help.
questions.answer: B
questions.note: 'And never breathe a word about your loss.'

questions.q: The poem has four stanzas of eight lines each.
questions.answer: A

questions.q: Kipling says one should walk with kings without losing the common touch.
questions.answer: A

questions.q: Risking all winnings on pitch-and-toss is meant literally as advice to gamble.
questions.answer: B
questions.note: It is a metaphor for taking a bold risk in life.

sections.title: Match the line with the quality it teaches ('If').

questions.left: Keep your head when all about you are losing theirs
questions.answer: Keep your head when all about you are losing theirs — Calmness in a crisis

questions.left: Trust yourself when all men doubt you
questions.answer: Trust yourself when all men doubt you — Self-confidence

questions.left: Walk with Kings — nor lose the common touch
questions.answer: Walk with Kings — nor lose the common touch — Humility

questions.q: If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two ________ just the same.
questions.answer: impostors

questions.q: If you can talk with crowds and keep your ________.
questions.answer: virtue

questions.q: If you can fill the unforgiving minute / With sixty seconds' worth of ________ run.
questions.answer: distance

questions.q: Yours is the Earth and everything that's in it, / And—which is more—you'll be a ________, my son!
questions.answer: Man

questions.q: Kipling was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in ________.
Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Are you going home?"
questions.answer: He asked me whether I was going home.

questions.q: Change into indirect speech: He asked me, "Which bus stops here?"
questions.answer: He asked me which bus stopped there.

questions.q: Change into indirect speech: My friend said, "What is your brother doing these days?"
questions.answer: My friend asked what my brother was doing those days.

questions.q: Change into indirect speech: My brother said, "Does Ram know my address?"
questions.answer: My brother asked whether Ram knew his address.

questions.q: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, "Did you finish your homework?"
questions.answer: She asked me if I had finished my homework.

questions.q: Name the device: 'Rage, rage against the dying of the light.'
questions.answer: Repetition (anaphora/refrain)

questions.q: Why does Kipling call 'Triumph' and 'Disaster' 'impostors'?
questions.answer: Neither lasts and neither shows the true value of a person. Success can make us proud and failure can crush us, so both deceive us; we should treat them alike.

questions.q: What does the poet mean by keeping or losing one's head?
questions.answer: Keeping one's head means staying calm and clear-minded in a crisis; losing it means panicking and acting without thought.

questions.q: Why should we not 'look too good, nor talk too wise'?
questions.answer: Because we should stay humble and natural. Pretending to be better or wiser than we are seems arrogant and self-righteous.

questions.q: What should we do in the face of failure, according to the poet?
questions.answer: We should start again from the beginning with whatever strength we have, without complaining, and rebuild what has been broken even with worn-out tools.

questions.q: What does 'not make dreams your master' mean?
questions.answer: We should dream and plan, but not let dreams rule us or lose touch with reality; we must also act practically.

questions.q: How can friends harm us? Why should 'none count too much'?
questions.answer: Loving friends can hurt us through our attachment and by misleading or disappointing us. If we depend too much on anyone we lose independence, so we should value all but rely on none too much.

questions.q: What is meant by 'fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run'?
questions.answer: Time never forgives waste; we should use every moment fully and purposefully, doing as much as we can in the time we have.

questions.q: What qualities does Kipling expect his son to have? List any four with reasons.
questions.answer: Calmness in crisis, so others' panic does not affect him; self-trust balanced with respect for others' doubts; patience and honesty — not lying or hating in return; and perseverance — starting again after losses and holding on by sheer will. These make him a mature 'Man'.

questions.q: How does the poem emphasise perseverance and determination?
questions.answer: It asks us to rebuild our broken life's work with worn-out tools, to start again after losing all our winnings without complaint, and to force heart, nerve and sinew to serve us long after they are spent, holding on by the Will alone.

or.q: What is the ultimate reward mentioned in the poem?
or.answer: If the son can fulfil all these 'ifs', the whole Earth and everything in it will be his — and, more important, he will become a true Man: mature, balanced and morally strong.

questions.q: Why is 'If' called a didactic poem?
questions.answer: A didactic poem teaches a lesson. Here a father instructs his son on how to live — staying calm, honest, humble, patient and determined — so that he becomes a mature man. The whole poem is a list of moral lessons.
